utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic. And good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to speak slowly and I would like to also ask you to make a break after my question for the benefit of the record. We want the record to reflect your words accurately. If you look at the transcript, you will also see the cursor. When the cursor stops, that means that the interpretation of the previous intervention is over. Mr. Andan, did you testify before this court in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the proofing in -- for your evidence in this case, did you have an occasion to listen to your testimony that you provided in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with the way your words have been recorded and do you still stand by the same positions, those that you offered when you testified in that case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm satisfied and I stand by every word that I said at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, the same ones that you were put by the Defence, the Trial Chamber, and the Prosecution in that case, would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D7370. 1D7370A is the confidential version of this document, whereas the former version is the public version of the document. I would like to tender the transcript into the evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. In addition to the transcripts, we have offered 40 associated exhibits and we would ask that they be added to our Rule 65 ter list as we had not decided to use his Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony at the time that list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. No objections whatsoever. I only wanted to mention that in relation to the associated exhibits, I found that many of the exhibits were not only referred to on the pages that are indicated in the 92 ter statement, but in addition they were also used and discussed on many other pages in particular during the cross-examination. Therefore, I have no objections against admission of all these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we upload 1D7430 referred to transcript pages 21662 and 21730. 1D7430. Do we not need an English translation -- oh, we have now English translation. Yes, when we checked there was none. That's fine. The Chamber has some concerns about the relevance of those -- the documents of the following: 1D7416; 1D7428, which is related to poker machine; and 1D7439. The Chamber finds those three documents not relevant so we'll not admit them. Otherwise, all the other documents will be admitted and will be given -- assigned an exhibit number by the Registrar in due course. Shall we assign the exhibit number for the two versions, both versions of the 92 ter transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 1D7370 will be Exhibit D3773, under seal, and 1D7370A will be Exhibit D3774.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think they might have reversed the public and confidential versions. The public version is 1D7370, so the one that should be under seal should be 1D7370A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's noted, Mr. Robinson. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read a short summary of Mr. Dragomir Andan's testimony. I'll do it in English. And then I'll ask him to answer a few additional questions with regard to some documents, mostly those he himself drafted and those are additional exhibits that have not yet been included in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Am I supposed to have a translation in Serbian or am I supposed to look at the document in English? Because I see it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You should be on channel 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's referring to the transcript that is on his -- the LiveNote that is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript, yes, the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have only English transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Dragomir Andan was born in Sarajevo on 12th of April, 1951. Serb by ethnicity, his step-father was Croat. He spent the majority of his career in the police since joining in 1976. He also used to be member of the communist party. He lived in an area of Sarajevo that was under Muslim control until leaving Sarajevo in April or May 1992. Until April 1992, and before the division of the MUP, Dragomir Andan held a position of a senior inspector first class at the MUP in Sarajevo. He was against the division of the MUP. After the multi-party elections in 1990, the situation became more complex as a -- personnel changes took place and those who had been in service for over 20 years have been replaced by people who in some cases were never in service before, which gave impression that professionalism no longer mattered. Personnel of MUP of each ethnicity had meetings of their own, in their offices or nearby restaurants. Dragomir Andan was not associated to any of these meetings. Dragomir Andan saw paramilitary groups, namely H-O-S, HOS, for the first time in September 1991 on his return from a task in Ljubuski. He transferred to the MUP of the Republika Srpska in May 1992, where he remained until August 1992 when he transferred to the military and began work in intelligence. Dragomir Andan was sent to Bijeljina and Brcko in May 1992 to rebuild public security stations structures of command and to introduce the working protocols. They acted -- a crew that was led by Mr. Andan acted in a highly professional manner, regardless of if it was petty theft or a grievous crime, such as murders, and also regardless of the perpetrator's ethnicity. Due to his -- due to this, they had ongoing struggles with local political structures as well as paramilitary groups, and the latter were often there just to loot for personal profit. Dragomir Andan addressed the highest authorities in the Republika Srpska as well as local authorities in Bijeljina to make them aware of constant struggle of Bijeljina SJB due to the paramilitary groups coming to the area and trying to destabilise SJB and its work. During Dragomir Andan's time in Bijeljina and Brcko, they took head of fight to try and dissolve and eliminate operations of paramilitary groups, namely Red Berets in Brcko, Mauzer's Panthers in Bijeljina, and Zuco's Yellow Wasps in Zvornik. However, although they managed to make many arrests of the paramilitary groups and their commanders, they were outnumbered and often threatened and approached with force for doing this. A police station in Janja was established, a predominantly Muslim village, where Muslims never left, in order to protect them from any threats posed by paramilitary groups in the area. During Dragomir Andan's period in Brcko, the SJB had no authority over the Luka collection centre. He had no knowledge of any Croat or Muslim civilians being detained at the premises of company called Laser, restaurant called Vestfalija, primary school in Loncari, DTV Partizan or co-operative store in Pelagicevo in Brcko. He became aware of Batkovic camp, in Bijeljina municipality, while in Brcko after inquiring about his friend Avdo -- Anto Vidovic. Dragomir Andan managed to get Vidovic released and employed in Brcko in police -- in Brcko police or military as a car electrician. He was a Croat. There were no other camps during his time in Bijeljina, although Batkovic was run by VRS, or rather, Eastern Bosnian Corps. There were no detention centres or camps held by MUP of the RS. Many reports of the working of SJB were sent to MUP; however, this was not always possible in a timely fashion due to the interruptions of dispatch -- in dispatch communication or in the phone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, let me ask you with regard ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- this. Can you tell us something about the crisis related to the position of the Chief of Staff of the public security station at Pale? You also testified about that in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, but if you will allow me, I believe that there has been a mistake in the interpretation. Anto Vidovic is not Anto Vidovic but Avdo Vidovic. He was at the Batkovic camp rather than in the Luka camp, as has been interpreted to me. I used the clout that I had with the commander of the East Bosnia Corps. I knew that Vidovic was there and I set him free from the Batkovic camp, not from the Luka camp, as has been interpreted to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I did say "Batkovic," but there was a mistake obviously. In the Stanisic evidence you spoke about the crisis related to the position of the Chief of Staff -- of chief of the public security station at Pale.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: May I? I'll try and rely on my memory to say something about that crisis which happened at Pale and involved the chief of the public security station, Mr. Malko Koroman. The minister of the interior, Mr. Mico Stanisic, was not happy with Mr. Malko Koroman's work, and I suppose that it was decided at the collegium meeting to remove Malko Koroman from that position and for him to be transferred somewhere else or for another duty to be assigned to him. From the moment that I learned about that - and I don't know how I learnt that - armed people started gathering around the police station at Pale. Their intention was not to allow the removal of Mr. Koroman and not to allow the inspectors who had brought the decision to give it to Mr. Koroman about his removal, not to hand it to him. As I stated before, about 3.000 people gathered there. Maybe I exaggerated the number a little, but I'm sure there were about 1.000 to 1500 armed people who were intent not to allow Mr. Koroman's removal. And then Mr. Karadzic intervened, as I've already stated. What I learnt is this: Mr. Karadzic's security detail as the president of the republic learned that armed persons had gathered around the police station. On the other hand, the legal powers, the police of Republika Srpska, were ready to disperse that crowd and to forcibly remove the chief of the police station. If that had happened, I'm sure that there would have been an armed conflict as a result of that. So the operative security asked Mr. Karadzic to be removed from Pale and to be transferred to a reserve position as we call it in our police jargon. However, another solution was found and the solution was this: One of the chiefs of security, I don't know which one, received instructions from Mr. Karadzic to go to the police station to try and appease the crowd and to see if they can be dispersed in a peaceful way so as to avoid conflicts. In other words, that the problem be resolved in a peaceful way. Luckily enough, the problem was resolved in that way. Mr. Koroman was told that he would not be removed, that the crowd would disperse, and the crowd did disperse. And shortly after that, I believe after three weeks, Mr. Koroman was transferred to another position in Bijeljina in a peaceful and legal way, and that's how the problem at Pale was resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. At transcript page 8, line 23, "the operative security asked Mr. Karadzic to be removed ..." I think that "Mr. Karadzic" should read "Mr. Koroman."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, Excellency, Karadzic to be displaced to the reserve post for the security reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go through this as briefly as possible. This sort of removal from position, was it normally within the purview of the relevant minister, to be able to change the personnel as he saw fit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, that's solely the power of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see that Koroman ultimately did remain on the police force. Now, did all this come about because of a criminal offence on his part or because the minister was unhappy with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, there was no criminal offence involved. Simply put, the minister wasn't happy with his work and dedication. He wanted to improve the performance of the service by bringing in someone who would be better at this job and who would improve the workings of the service. In that way, the service would simply take a new course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you were a member of the SDS and if you had been asked to join the party in order that you may remain in your position or be promoted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I had never been a member of any party ever since my departure from the League of Communists, and I am not a member of any party today. I was never asked to join the SDS in order that I may retain any office that I held or may be assigned to any new office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've extensively talked about your mission in Brcko. I would like to show you a document of yours so that you can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D0937. It is the only document that hasn't been translated and that we will use, but it is not a lengthy document. I'll ask Mr. Andan to tell us what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this? It's the 23rd of January, especially the second paragraph, if you could read it out aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: "The situation relating to the paramilitary forces in Zvornik has not been resolved. For this reason," there's a smudge there, "our forces have been engaged on this to a large extent" -- oh, now I understand. So I'll resume. "The situation relating to the paramilitary forces in Brcko and Zvornik has not been resolved, and for that reason our forces are to a large extent engaged on this issue rather than in combat."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does the heading say? We see that it says "Security Services Centre Bijeljina." Can we see the signature block?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Can it be scrolled down, please. Yes, this is my document. It's a dispatch or a telegram. So it was sent out encoded. This is one of the daily or weekly situation reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that the interpretation was the other way around in transcript, that -- it seems to say -- oh, it's because "the situation relating to the paramilitary forces has not been resolved because our forces are to a large extent engaged in combat rather than on pursuing these paramilitaries." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3810, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness another document, it's 1D09138 and it's dated the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the document and can you tell us if you remember what this is about? Paragraph 3, you report that the special unit arrived in Brcko; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you briefed the political structures on what needed to be done and agreed on what would be done. Can you tell us at this point in time, on the 24th of July, who was the authority in Brcko for all intents and purposes? I don't mean de jure, I mean de facto. Could the local authorities be in charge of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: If you'll allow me a short introduction, let me say, first of all, that this is a daily report that we sent to the Ministry of the Interior. As for the second paragraph, the Ministry of the Interior is being informed about the fact that that very morning, at around 4.00 or 5.00, we arrived in Brcko with the special unit in order to try and eliminate - I don't mean physically - but remove the paramilitary forces that were rampant in Brcko at the time. Now, what you asked me a moment ago, let me say that the authorities were not able to be in control of all the levers of power, as it were, because these paramilitary forces were a constant threat to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph about intelligence work, what sort of intelligence work was this? You came to know that they had not yet been subordinated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can Mr. Karadzic repeat his question and the witness his answer. It is going too fast and they are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, and before Mr. Karadzic repeats his question, it was very leading so he should actually also change what he asks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Probably you have noted the interpreter's request not to overlap each other. If you could repeat your question and not in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what does this document report about and what does the last sentence mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: As I've already said, we arrived in the municipality of Brcko in order to eliminate - and I said not in the physical sense - the paramilitary group of the Red Berets who were rampant in the town, looting, spreading unrest and turmoil in every respect. As we arrived in Brcko, we had several meetings with representatives of the authorities and the army. What followed next was that we gave an indirect ultimatum to the members of the Red Berets that, by 1800 hours of that day, they should be resubordinated to the army and that they should receive all their further orders from the army and be part and parcel of that body. We also said that they should not operate independently. On that and the following day, we engaged -- well, it was also previously that we engaged in intelligence work in order to gain as much information about them as possible. And we continued that sort of intelligence work as we arrived there in order to supplement the information we already had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The English interpretation is finished. Please explain to us, does resubordination to the army exonerate those among their members who committed criminal offences and what does this last sentence in the document mean, that work should continue on the collection of documents and investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: We first gathered them at the barracks so that they may formally be resubordinated to the army. We next resumed our intelligence work to find out what sort of criminal offences they had committed in the previous period so that they may be prosecuted. Our part of the job was to collect information and put together a criminal report that we would file with the competent prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 13, line 17, when you listed the misdeeds that they did, among other things you said lack of respect for human rights, and this did not find its way into the transcript. Did you list among their sins also the lack of respect for human rights?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3811, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if there were cases of murder where perpetrators were known and what was the position that your service took in that respect in Bijeljina and Brcko? Can you recall a case or, let's say, the case of one Kukic who was murdered.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: As for Brcko, I don't remember. As far as Bijeljina is concerned, I do remember that four members who were of Serb ethnicity perpetrated the murder of Salko Kukic. It was murder for personal gain. They killed him and stole around 120.000 German marks off him. As soon as we learned of this crime, we arrested these individuals. As an aside, let me say that we carried out all the necessary police work, we secured the scene of crime, examined it. And then, as a result of our investigatory work, we identified the perpetrators, located them soon thereafter, brought them in to the police station in Bijeljina, obtained custody for them, took written statements from them, and handed these statements over to the prosecution. Let me tell you that trial did not ensue directly after these events, nor did -- nor were these individuals remanded into custody. However, the documentation that we gathered in 1992 was re-activated in 2006 or 2007, and these individuals are currently serving their sentences for that particular case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D09134.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, is this the criminal report that you submitted? Do you recall the first page? Four perpetrators are listed on page 1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I remember the family name by Pojatar, because it's very peculiar, Istok Pojatar and that is the criminal report in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The victim, Kukic, what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Muslim or, as they say, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Beneath the accused it is stated that they are reported here because they killed Salko Kukic at about 2230 hours on the 2nd of June, 1992. Is that the criminal offence that we discussed? And that it was committed for personal gain.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did say so a moment ago. Based on what we came to learn subsequently, Salko came from a wealthy family. They probably learned of a sizeable amount of jewellery and money that he had on him and decided to commit this criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you chief of the public security station in Bijeljina at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I arrived in Bijeljina after I had completed my mission in Brcko. I was police inspector at the time. Seeing that there was not enough personnel in Bijeljina to fill the vacant posts, under-secretary Cedo Kljajic, who was in Bijeljina at the time, asked me that I should -- aside from being inspector, and that was the training that I had at the time, that I should also be chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3812, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D09136.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you put them into custody and who had the authority of remanding them in detention three days later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, the document shows that police custody was extended of -- the police custody of 72 hours which was provided under Law on Criminal Procedure. Now, upon the expiry of the police custody, it is the prosecutor who can either extend the term of detention or have the individual released. As you were able to see in this line of documents, we carried out the investigation activities. We took them into custody, and for the remainder of the procedure, the individual was in the hands of the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3813, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D09135.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have seen what the reason was and that it was done pursuant to Article 6, which is murder, in the case of Rodic. Can you tell us now what was the reason for detaining this individual pursuant to Article 165, and towards the bottom it says that there were grounds for suspicion that this was done, but that he didn't report it. Was it his duty to report that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, he was obliged to file a report, and he failed to do that this is considered complicity to the commission of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he was prosecuted for harbouring and concealing the facts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, he was put in detention as well and his case file was prepared and forwarded to the prosecutor for further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3814, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please now explain in more detail what was the role of police and your personal role after the arrest of the Wasps and at which point your responsibility ended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: After having collected all the intelligence relating to the activities of the paramilitary formation called the Yellow Wasps, the State Security Service and a few members of the public security service, led by me at the time, were carrying out surveillance of all the facilities where members of the Yellow Wasps were staying. We collected intelligence about their activities in which they were involved in the area of Zvornik municipality. We compiled and drew up an operational plan and carried out the arrest of the Yellow Wasps by bringing them into the responsible centre, and I think that it already existed, that was the centre in Bijeljina, where they were processed, which means that they were put in detention for 72 hours, written statements were taken from them, case files were completed, a criminal file was -- a criminal report was filed with the prosecutor's office. And the prosecutor's office in Bijeljina took over the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened with the items that they had looted which you confiscated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: All the items that we found inside the facilities as well as the motor vehicles that they had plundered, we confiscated them against receipt on temporary confiscation. We used the gym to store smaller items at the CSB Bijeljina, and as for the vehicles, we also stored them in a depot that was secured by the police because inside this compound were not only the vehicles that we confiscated during the mopping-up operation of Yellow Wasps and there were other vehicles there as well, and smaller items, as I said, were stored in the Bijeljina CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the further procedure regarding the items whose owners were identified?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: We had a case of a certain Simic, a jeweller from Zvornik. He was also a member of the Yellow Wasps. During the search of his premises and his residence, we found a large quantity of gold which we catalogued and we gave his wife a receipt confirming that we had confiscated the said items. On that occasion we also confiscated a BMW car from Mr. Simic in order to make some check because we thought that that was also the subject of a crime. Later on, through the processing procedure and after Mr. Simic was released from detention, he provided documents about the origin of the gold, stating that it was taken from his jeweller's store and that the BMW had been purchased before the war on which he had proper papers. We returned all these items, the gold and the vehicle, and issued a proper certificate on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at 1D092 -- 9132.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened with the items that were really looted and found in the possession of members of the Yellow Wasps? Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document. Through intelligence work we obtained partial information as to which houses were robbed by members of the Yellow Wasps, and this is a document that was sent to the public security station in Zvornik and these items were handed over to them in order for them to be returned to their original owners. Now it is stated here that everything that has been stolen from known premises and houses should be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The people who were robbed, what was their ethnicity, the majority of them, the people robbed by the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Most of them were Muslims. But in the course of this bestial conduct, once they ran out of Muslim houses they switched to robbing Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3815, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D09133. It's 1D09133.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this document and can you tell us what is the ethnicity of the person under number 1 in paragraph 3. Her name is Hasnija. Let me just remind you that this is the same date as the previous document, which is the 13th of August.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document. Hasnija was a Muslim or a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So all the questions you asked is whether Ms. Coric is a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him whether he remembered this document as being the one produced by him and what it pertains to, but it is a follow-up of the previous document which was a self-explanatory one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Andan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can confirm that. As Mr. Karadzic said, this is a follow-up document and it pertains to the return of items to the owners from whom members of the Yellow Wasps confiscated or robbed them of - I don't know how to qualify it - and it contains instructions that I provided as the chief to the effect that these items should be returned to the persons named in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3816, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know and did you provide occasional reports to the Presidency and did you know what was my opinion with regard to your action and to the existence of paramilitary in general?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I spent seven or eight years in the State Security Service or the so-called secret police of the former Yugoslavia, or rather, of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The way we were trained was that once we face complex problems we should provide reports to the top echelons of the Bosnia-Herzegovina leadership. At the time these kind of reports were written and addressed to the central committee, to the Presidency, and to the prime minister of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Having been trained to pursue this practice, when I came to Semberija and Majevica and after we had evaluated the total political situation, on two occasions I sent reports to the leadership of Republika Srpska about the huge amount of problems and the security and political situation prevailing in the area of Republika Srpska, specifically Majevica and Semberija. In that context, two letters were sent to Mr. President, Mr. Karadzic. My wish and intention was to draw the attention of the leadership to the situation that prevailed in Semberija and Majevica at the time. Our objective was to inform the political leadership of Republika Srpska and provide documents to that effect so that they can have an insight into the situation in Semberija and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P29002 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any feedback information as to enjoying support for the actions that you were taking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did receive feedback information, notably from Prime Minister Stanisic, to the effect that you were supportive of all the actions that we were taking in Semberija and Majevica. However, I'm not sure whether you put your own comment on one report and I think I saw it after the war anyway. Mr. Stanisic told me that we enjoyed full support of the leadership of Republika Srpska and that they expected us to continue with our activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that one of the two reports that you sent me on or around the date of the arrest?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, this is a cover letter that was attached to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at the last page. It is already in evidence but I need the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read the portion that is handwritten.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: "Continue with restoring law and order and" -- I'm sorry, I can't read this word. "Continue with restoring law and order."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Law and order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, and there's your signature underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, did you respond in a certain way to the request by the president of Republika Srpska relating to the existence of a camp for captured and imprisoned persons and the treatment of these individuals? Do you remember receiving anything about that and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the last part of the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters couldn't catch the last part of your question, Mr. Karadzic. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did you receive any inquiries from the ministry and did you act accordingly with regard to the East Bosnia Corps? Did you send a request to receive a report about the situation in order to enable you to provide a response?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, a dispatch came from the Ministry of the Interior. In that dispatch, they wanted answers about collection centres possibly kept by the police. All the information about such facilities had to be conveyed to the Ministry of the Interior. If my memory serves me well, that was the issue. We answered that in the territory of the Bijeljina CSB there were no such collection centres or camps. As far as I can remember, we told them that there was the Batkovic camp and that that camp was under the authority of the military and that they should seek information from the military. Within that context, a dispatch arrived and we responded to that dispatch in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D09141 is the document I would like to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this how you learnt about Batkovic? Is that how you managed to set that Croat, Vidovic, free? We have the document. Please look at it. Is this a document that somebody signed on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, it is only logical when the number one person is absent a document is signed by his deputy. I don't know who signed it, but I stand by the document. Obviously we sent this document to the East Bosnia Corps, asking them to respond to the dispatch that had been sent to us by the ministry. When the dispatch arrived, since I do not hail from Bijeljina, I asked my colleagues to gather intelligence to see whether there was a collection centre or a camp in the territory of Bijeljina. I was told that there was Batkovic; however, the military was in charge, the military of Republika Srpska. And then the dispatch that we received from the Ministry of the Interior was forwarded to the East Bosnia Corps. We asked them to provide certain explanations or provide details about the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of August, 1992, was that camp made accessible? Did the leadership learn about that camp as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I don't know what leadership you had in mind; however, if you had in mind the leadership of the police station, I would like to say that we did not get involved in that. If you meant the leadership of the republic itself, I'm sure that you were provided with adequate explanation with regard to the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3817, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now in very general terms, can you tell us something about the period with regard to law and order and the abilities of the authorities to manage the processes until the end of August. Tell us from your perspective, from as much as you could glean into the authorities of the civilian segment of the power.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: It all depended on the organisation of municipalities and police stations that existed there. When Muslims prevailed in a police station, when they retired, they left a big void in the police stations. And that was largely used by the paramilitaries that were headed by known criminals. At that moment, they sensed there was an opportunity to amass large wealth by looting and robbing. In certain municipalities, during the first stage of the war there was a state of lawlessness. Despite the legally elected powers, they did not have the real leverage to oppose such paramilitary formations. That was particularly true of Brcko, and I believe you will find it in my testimony in Stanisic. I sent a dispatch on behalf, or rather, the Ministry of the Interior sent a dispatch to send me to Brcko in order to consolidate the situation there and to consolidate the ranks in the Brcko police station. It was impossible for the legally elected authorities to exert authority since they didn't have real leverage. The situation was somewhat better in Bijeljina, but the situation was somewhat similar in the territory of the Zvornik municipality. Therefore, it was very difficult for all those who were members of the executive powers to actually exercise their duties because the police did not function as well as they should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the transcript there is a reference to a situation when Muslims came to you to complain about the activities of groups and individuals. Can you tell us, who did Muslims fear? Could they find assistance and could they find refuge in the police stations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "civilians of Muslim ethnicity," but very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, again we have a transcript reference because you didn't provide us with the reference of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I would firstly ask Mr. Andan to answer while I'm looking for this reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, Mr. Andan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, yes, I can. There were several such examples, but I remember a very striking one. In Bijeljina, a person came to the police station, a Muslim or a Bosniak. I know that he was a veterinarian. He complained about being been stopped by paramilitaries who stole his private car, a Golf. We filed his complaint. Police officers from Bijeljina went there and we quickly found those persons who stole the car. We invited the gentleman in question, we returned the car to him, and a report was sent to the prosecutor's office about those persons. There were many such examples. I happened to reside in Bijeljina at the time. One night, my neighbour, Amir Fidahic was attacked. I personally intervened at that moment. Again there were members of paramilitaries who wanted to enter Mr. Fidahic's house. I suppose they wanted to rob him or do something else to him, perhaps even murder him, God forbid. And I came out of the house where I lived. During that time my wife called the police. We disarmed four or five persons, members of that paramilitary group. We took them to the police station and that's how the situation ended. There were several such examples, but these are the two that I remember as very striking examples of the situation as it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your information. The first example can be found on page 21453. Mr. Andan, on page 21441, you mention that Brcko was an affluent town and you say the same about Bijeljina and Zvornik. Can you tell us, did you establish a correlation between the wealth of a municipality and the presence of paramilitary formations? In other words, were there any paramilitaries in Lopare and other poor municipalities, as it were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Brcko municipality was the second- or the third-most developed municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were a lot of economic activities going on in Brcko. There was the food industry and other industries. Bijeljina was also rich due to its agricultural resources. And as for Zvornik, it had several factories which were of strategic importance for Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. Through our intelligence analysis, we learned that all those paramilitary formations that arrived in the territory of Republika Srpska arrived precisely in those developed municipalities because they could loot there, they could obtain property, and they could amass wealth in a very quick way. Nobody wanted to go to Cajnice, Kalinovik, Nevesinje, and some other underdeveloped municipalities. They chose their targets well. They chose wealthy municipalities because their main objective was not warfare and helping Serbian fighters who were fighting for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their main goal was to loot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And finally, my last question, Mr. Andan, before the break. Can you please tell us, as a professional did you do things that you personally didn't like? However, did you act as a professional in every situation? You can just say yes or no, and then I'm going to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's how I was trained, that's how I was brought up. Whatever I do, I have to do it professionally. In every situation, even in the gravest war-time situation, I acted as a professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember when the Law on Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal was adopted? As the chief of the CSB Eastern Sarajevo, did you act in accordance with that law?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when the Law on The Hague Tribunal was adopted. But I know that as the chief of centre and as the director of the police of the MUP of Republika Srpska, I implemented that law in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D09139. There's no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your document. Could you please present the document to us in the light of the previous question that you've just answered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we first see the heading, the top of the page, where you can see that the date is the 29 of October, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you the chief of the public security centre in Serbian Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, at that time I was the chief of the CSB in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber and the other participants what is the nature of this document in the light of the previous question about the implementation of the Law on Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal? Since there is no translation, could you either read the document or could you give us a summary of the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I can give you a summary or I can read it. I don't know what is easier for you and for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Give us a summary because a translation will follow. Just tell us about the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: This document was sent to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. It represents and it sends them things that we found at Famos-Koran where your office was for a certain while. We found some disks and the film "Sarajevo: The beginning and the end." We found six items at the Famos premises and we handed them over to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be marked for identification? This brings my examination-in-chief to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could help the Chamber in terms of relevance, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps Dr. Karadzic could address this, but it seems like it goes to the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, Mr. Robinson is right. Before us we have a professional who acts professionally in every situation, regardless of the recipient of his information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll -- yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree, it -- when you read the transcript of his testimony, a lot of portions dealing with conduct of Mr. Andan in the later years, and therefore I think it has some relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3818, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break and after which we will hear the cross-examination. But before we break, the Chamber will turn to the accused's motion -- motions to subpoena Ratko Mladic and Mico Stanisic filed respectively on the 18th of April, 2013, and the 24th of June, 2013. The Chamber recalls that on the 4th of June, 2013, it granted, by majority, Zdravko Tolimir's application to appeal the Chamber's decision issuing a subpoena compelling him to testimony, and stayed the execution of the said subpoena pending resolution of the issue by the Appeals Chamber. The Chamber further recalls that on the 2nd of July, 2013, it decided to postpone the testimony of two subpoenaed witnesses currently involved in appeal proceedings at the Tribunal, i.e., Ljubisa Beara and Radivoje Miletic, pending resolution of this issue by the Appeals Chamber. Accordingly, the Chamber has decided to stay its determination on the Mladic and the Mico Stanisic subpoena motions pending resolution of the Tolimir's appeal by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just raise one other brief matter which involves a response we received on Wednesday from the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the availability of two witnesses for whom we have requested transfer to The Hague for testimony as Defence witnesses, Franc Kos and Mendeljejev Djuric. Given the response of the government, we would ask the Trial Chamber take steps to bring both of these witnesses so that they can arrive by the 25th of July and can give testimony in this case on the 29th of July. Those dates vary from those that we had previously submitted in our written motion, and given the circumstances, we think it's better that we have that testimony on those dates. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 11.06.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I had one scheduling matter I wanted to raise. I didn't think it was necessary, nor did Mr. Robinson, to leave the witness in the witness room for that purpose. The quick backdrop to this is simply my earlier indications concerning the testimony of the expert witness Mr. Keserovic. The other day I recited the circumstances surrounding the acceleration of his testimony first from September and then to an even earlier date that left us essentially about a week to deal with his testimony. The Court kindly indicated that it was inclined to grant that request but wanted to see how it evolved and whether it would be possible to go directly to cross. I considered that that basically implicated two possibilities: One, the nature of the direct; and two, the impact of the preparations that took place in the meantime. With respect to the direct examination, that really didn't feature in our assessment of the impossibility of proceeding and I think was not -- we didn't consider that the nature of the direct was part of that request. So I wanted to let the Court know that with respect to the efforts thus far, we did engage in the most intensive possible preparation since we learned of the accelerated testimony, and I thought it was important then to advise the Court that it has now become clear that notwithstanding those accelerated and intensive efforts, that it would not be possible to proceed with cross-examination on Tuesday without really unfairly impacting the Prosecution's examination and the quality and extent of the information the Court would -- is entitled to receive and expects to receive. I spoke to Mr. Robinson about this. Our proposal is that we defer the cross-examination to the very beginning of the next week. I think he considers this, under the circumstances, to be a fair request and -- but would, of course, leave it to the Trial Chamber to determine the schedule. I raise this for a couple of reasons, not the least of which is some measure of certainty as we undertake the remaining portions of the examination -- of the preparation in hope -- hopefully in an organised and rational fashion and one that doesn't have the -- those preparing the cross-examination here engaged in sleepless nights from now until Tuesday, rather than trying to engage in a more methodical and rational preparation of the cross. So I would ask that the Court make that decision and indicate that the cross-examination can be postponed until the beginning of the following week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. The Chamber finds that it is fair enough. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, the testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin trial that was accepted by the Trial Chamber this morning is very detailed and there is no need to repeat the evidence you provided in that trial. I only want to address some aspects of your previous testimony. And as the time that we have for the cross-examination is limited, I would kindly ask you to give short answers and focusing on the question that I ask. And if I need more details, then I will ask you additional questions on that particular topic. Mr. Andan, in -- during the testimony in the other case - and I refer here to page 21368 - and also this morning, you described that after the multi-party election and the subsequent changes in the political structure, professionalism in the police did not count any longer when a new post or a post was to be changed; it was rather a matter of party affiliation that was the most important factor. That applied to all three sides, correct? It was the same for the Muslims, for the Croats, and for the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I think that you are partly right. I will try to explain this and I will try to be as short as you asked me to be. Let me tell you that at the lower levels of authorities - I mean municipalities - you are practically right. As for the Serb personnel, at the top of the pyramid, let's say the Ministry of the Interior, professionalism was honoured, if I can put it that way. All the personnel who were appointed to senior positions and who were of Serb ethnicity were individuals who had been working in the Ministry of the Interior before. This, however, was not the case where individuals of Bosniak ethnicity were involved as well as Croat. So I'm -- I was talking about the top of the pyramid. Now, if we talk about the lower level, that's where you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But these positions that were changed and filled with other people, on the higher level that was agreed beforehand between the political parties; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I am not in a position to say that this was the case or that it was not the case. If we take the position of the head of personnel of the MUP and if that position is taken by a person who was director or manager of a brewery, then, as a result, you may infer that it must have been a political arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was asking this, actually, because you said exactly that, that positions -- appointments were, in fact, agreed upon beforehand by political parties. You said that in your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, and that is at page 21378. So I took it that at that time when you gave this testimony you told the truth and that is what you remembered; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: You are right. I did say that earlier on. Of course, the command structure, as it were, was changed in the Ministry of the Interior and of course the Serb, Muslim, and Croat individuals who took up these positions did so with the previous approval of political parties. And the positions were filled depending on the agreement between the political parties, and of course again it depended on whether this should be the Croat, Serb, or Muslim. If me as a Serb were to take up the position of the head of administration, which according to the power-sharing agreement fell to Serbs, then of course I would take that position and it was the result of the agreement of the political authorities. This, however, did not mean that I had to be a member of that party as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to remind you, be very brief because these details you have already given in your testimony. In the beginning of the war, even persons with criminal records were recruited into the Serb police force, such as in the Serb police in Bijeljina and even more so in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I don't recall stating that the police forces in Sarajevo recruited individuals with a criminal record. However, we did have persons who were recruited into the police forces in Brcko and Bijeljina, even in Zvornik, and that much is true; however, for Sarajevo, I don't recall that any of the posts in my republican MUP were taken by -- well, I know that they -- some of them were taken by Muslims with a criminal record. So I can vouch for that. I know that they were, indeed, taken on. I know their names as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into these details. I just was remembering that you said that -- not in your testimony, that's right, but you gave two interviews to the Office of the Prosecutor, one in Brcko and one in Banja Luka. And we will come to some of the things that you said in these statements today. Mr. Andan, in your testimony you refer to the mistrust in the police along ethnic lines and you gave a lot of details and we don't need to repeat that. For the participants here it's on page 21377. This mistrust and antagonism was not only among the police, but in fact developed in the entire populations in Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Can you be a bit more specific, if possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The nationalist parties and their leaders created an atmosphere of mistrust and fear of the other ethnic groups in their speeches; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I would not phrase it that way. This is my answer. Naturally from a system which propagated brotherhood and unity, we ended up with a multi-party system which divided the ethnicities, I mean the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. As for my service, of course, with the arrival of some new individuals who were suspect of certain reports coming from the ground because they came from the Serbs, this created a degree of mistrust because these reports were judged by whether or who they were sent by. At the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, these were political issues, and as a policeman I don't want to discuss that. So I can state for a fact that as for the service, yes, this was the case. There was a certain degree of mistrust among the individuals working there with the introduction of a multi-party system in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you got information that with the help of the nationalist parties - and I'm referring here to the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA - people were arming themselves; right? You got that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that was the case. We received reports, though these were mostly off-the-record reports, unofficially, that I was informed that members of the three ethnicities were being armed and that weapons were being distributed to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25237 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that, Mr. Andan, is a report of the interview you had with the investigators in Brcko, the ICTY investigators in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And unfortunately, we have it only in English because it was not translated. Can we please have page 3 and we look first at the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in that second paragraph you say -- you speak about the Serbs having strong ties with the TO and the JNA and even sold weapons to the Croats and the Muslims, and that the national parties were involved in the arming of the public. That was recorded by the investigators that interviewed you. That is how you described it in 2005; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask one thing? Since this is an English text, shouldn't the witness be told that these are not his words but an interpretation of his words, "Andan stated," et cetera. So these are not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be read out, and if he finds some question he can clarify with the Prosecution. And you can -- but he understands what this is -- this is a statement he gave and written in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I actually told Mr. Andan that it was recorded in this way by the investigators, a report -- they made a report out of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, so can you answer the question, please? Is that what you had experienced and gotten the information about, Serbs having strong ties to the TO and JNA, even selling weapons to the other sides, and the national parties were involved in the arming of the public?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I would like to clarify one thing about this document. I think it would have been logical for me to have written this document and signed it, rather than making an interpretation of it or, as we called it, to make an official note of it. That would have been the right way to have taken my statement, written it down, and for me to have signed it. However, let me give you my comment on this. It is correct that I had an interview in Brcko with The Hague Tribunal investigators. I'm not denying that. I'm afraid that my interpretation was not faithfully reflected. Perhaps something was taken out of context. Now, specifically the question that you were discussing, is it correct that the Serbs had strong or stronger ties with the JNA and the Territorial Defence? Well, it all depended on the territory where the TO storage facilities were. Quite a few of these storage facilities with weapons and ammunition were located in the territory of the Croatian and Bosniak entity. For instance, there was one in Busovaca, and they - that's to say, Muslims and Croats - were able to get armed easily from there. Now, the storage facilities which were located on the territory of the Serbs, it was only logical that they should be arming themselves out of these. It is also logical that members of the JNA where the majority of the officers were Serbs helped more, to a greater extent, the Serb population than the Croat or Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph in this document there is a reference - and I quote you from the documents, that is, what the investigator have written down, that you said - "The national parties created an atmosphere of mistrust and constant reminders of what happened in World War II and reinforced that they would never allow this to happen again." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I entirely reject this statement. I don't think I said this. I would be happy if there was an audio recording of this. As for the arming, well, I did state that and I explained the context in which I did. Now, this statement, referring to the Second World War and that the national parties spread propaganda among the people in this way, I fully reject this allegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this page please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we don't have any objection. It was read out. I'm not SO sure if there's any value to it, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, did you say that it was a tape-recorded interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it was not a tape-recorded interview. It was an information report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Information report. The Chamber was discussing how to assess this probative value when witness denies having said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether -- yes, yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, he has actually agreed to one part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is the previous paragraph, and he has denied the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, for our part we don't disagree that it can be admitted and weighed by the Chamber. It's -- although it's not his words, it's someone else's statement of his words, you can give it whatever weight you think it deserves, and obviously it deserves a lot less weight than if we had a recording or something signed by the witness. But nevertheless, I think our practice has been to admit this kind of evidence if you think it's necessary to have a written version of what was read out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit the first page and this page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please have 65 ter 25230 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Andan, we do have a taped interview that you gave to the ICTY investigators in Banja Luka. And we have actually just made excerpts from a very, very lengthy -- very lengthy interview. And I will only address a few pages of it, therefore we made this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If we look at page 6, page 6, in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S, please. And in the English we look at the end of the first paragraph -- no, I think there's something -- I think there's something wrong. It would need to be the page which says English 111. The B/C/S is correct but the English is not. 110, it's 110.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I had a mistake. It needs to be 5 also for the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as I said, we look -- in the English we look at the end of the first -- we look at the end of the big paragraph at the lower part. And in the B/C/S we look at the second paragraph -- the second half of that page in B/C/S. In the context of the criminals in the police in various parts, that's the topic that was also addressed, towards the criminal police officers, you say the following: "I must say something, that the war in Sarajevo was commenced -- was started together with Momcilo Mandic by criminals" -- I can't find this right now ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- the previous, page 6, was correct. Page 6 was correct. Page 6 in the English. And in the B/C/S it is page 5. And if you look at the end of the second paragraph in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Andan, you have to look at the lower part -- the lower part of the B/C/S. And you are recorded here as saying: "I must say something, that the war in Sarajevo was commenced -- was started together with Momcilo Mandic by criminals." Are you here referring to the erection of the first barricades beginning in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you refer to Mr. Mandic and the criminals, are you referring to Rajko Djukic here or who do you mean by "criminals"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not mentioning Rajko Djukic. You actually -- you might mean Rajko Dukic, though I didn't mention him anywhere. I did hear of him at the time. Now, these fir barricades that were organised in the month of March with the assistance of criminals, most of whom I knew, they manned the barricades at the time. Later on, through intelligence work in the joint MUP, it was learned that Momcilo Mandic sent these criminals to erect the barricades in March in Sarajevo. To the best of my recollection, I don't mention Rajko Dukic at all; I didn't know him at the time. Did I hear of him at the time? I'm not sure. I got to know him in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "criminals," whom do you mean then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, let me not engage in guess-work. Let me mention the late Skrba, the late Rato, the late Vule, they were all individuals with a criminal record in our ministry whom we arrested and took into custody at some point and they were the ones who were manning these barricades in Sarajevo. There are others that I can't recall at present, I remembered these three, but if you want me to I can tell you specifically who these -- or which of these criminals they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think that's actually sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this page admitted and we will have in the course of this testimony several more small bits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. We'll admit the first page -- but let us see the first page has been separately -- no. We'll admit this page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6434.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you upload the first page later on. That would be more convenient to find out what interview it was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, you describe in your written evidence - and I refer here to 21381 for everybody in court - you describe in a lot of details of the barricades and we do not need to repeat them. I was just wondering about something you said on page 21384 because -- and that's why I asked about Rajko Dukic. You state that Rajko Dukic was the chief of Crisis Staff and he and Momcilo Mandic were the organisers of the barricades on the 1st and the 2nd of March. And you also stated on page 21386 that Rajko Dukic was in charge of personnel affairs in the SDS. So when you gave your testimony, you mentioned him in the context of the barricades. I assume you knew him -- you knew that it better then when you gave your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I already said that only later did we acquire certain intelligence information that a certain Rajko Dukic was at the head of the Crisis Staff that was leading the campaign of setting up barricades in Sarajevo. Later I heard - and you can ask President Karadzic about that as well - that he was the president of what was called maybe the personnel commission in the party, and that is something that I also learned later. That's what I learned from intelligence report. But I must tell you the following. When the barricades were erected in Sarajevo I was a member of the Ministry of the Interior of BH, i.e., the joint ministry. That night we received an order to assemble at the MUP without knowing what the problem was. We didn't know anything about the barricades. The barricades appeared in the morning and we learned about that only later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I stopped you because that -- all these details we have already in the testimony and we do not need to repeat this because we, unfortunately, do not have the time to do so. Mr. Andan, in your testimony you describe in many, many details what you and Mr. Davidovic's tasks were and your activities in relation to Bijeljina and we do not need to repeat this here. I only was puzzled by something you said in relation to Ljubisa Savic, nicknamed Mauzer, and his Panthers. And you refer also to Vojvoda Mirko Blagojevic and his men as the most significant paramilitary formations in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, is on page 21437.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I was only puzzled about one point because you refer to the troops commanded, if I can call it that, by Vojvoda Blagojevic were called Serb Volunteers -- Volunteer Guard. And I was just wondering whether that's an error, because in the course of your testimony you then refer to Arkan's men as being the Serb Volunteer Guards. Could that be a -- just an error?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: There must have been a mistake made. They were Mirko Blagojevic's Chetnik and the Serbian Volunteer Guards was led by Arkan, and I apologise if I made an error.
