utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just saw it and wanted to have you -- give you an opportunity to correct that. And there was -- you also mentioned on page 21653 that there was a link between Arkan's Serb Volunteer Guard and Ljubisa Savic's Panthers. Do you know -- do you remember that, that there was that link?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that when I arrived in Bijeljina that there were certain complications. Somebody, not me, informed Arkan that Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, was constantly hiding behind his name. I remember one afternoon when Arkan came to Bijeljina and said in front of me and Mico Blagojevic that he had nothing to do with Mauzer and he pleaded with us to act according to the law with regard to the Mauzer, but there had been some links between the two in the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, when I read the evidence on your achievements in Bijeljina and Brcko and Zvornik and I also read the associated documentation that was discussed in that testimony, I was a bit puzzled about the strong focus on looting and robbery while one would think that the focus on violent crimes like rapes and killings would be the focus of the police work. Why was it looting and robbery rather than the more serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I am not sure that you perceived the entire situation in a correct way with regard to what I did in the area. I am sorry that in my file there is a rape of a Muslim woman, and I think that Mr. Davidovic can confirm this, and I can confirm that we filed a report to the court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, if you could speak a bit more slowly and then could you repeat after you said, "We filed a report to the court ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We filed a report to the prosecutor's office for the rape of a Muslim woman in Bijeljina, and that can be corroborated by Mr. Mico Davidovic. As for the other part relating to the looting, I believe that those were the most serious crimes at the time. How can one explain such instances when a member of a paramilitary unit comes to a Muslim house, kicks the door with his foot or with his rifle, force his way into the house, make a search, collect all the valuables, and leave? I can tell you that any such instance could not have gone by without the owner of the house suffering maltreatment in the process. And that is what we considered as the most serious criminal offences at the time and we wanted to provide protection to all the individuals living in those municipalities in the period, and I am talking about Brcko, Bijeljina, and Zvornik. So we processed other individuals as well, and we were careful that people who were coming back from the front line be searched at the check-points around Bijeljina and to confiscate any stolen items from them and deposit them in our storage facilities. For example, at one of the check-points we stopped an active-duty officer of the Army of Republika Srpska and we confiscated a truck full of stolen goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I asked this question because here in front of this Trial Chamber we had Exhibit P2882, it's actually your charging document from 8 August 1992 for the Yellow Wasps. And in this document it is all about stealing cars and goods -- and goods at the check-points and using false papers for stolen cars. And what I was missing in this charging document were the crimes that -- the crimes against the Muslims in Celopek. That is why I was thinking you were concentrating on robbery and stealing only. Why is that not in here, the murder of the Muslims at Celopek?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I must tell you this and it can be verified. Given that many people fled from the state of Serbia, during our action many of them fled back to Serbia, and as a result we passed over many documents to the MUP of Serbia and based on which Zuco's brother - I think his last name was Repic - was tried and he was convicted by a court in Sabac in -- or Valjevo to ten years in prison on the basis of the documents that we provided to the court. I'm not saying that our documents were a decisive factor in filing a criminal report against Repic. So you are right in the first part of your question, but I wanted to say that since certain individuals were in Serbia at the time, we provided the documents relating to them to the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 3, it has been erroneously recorded that they fled from Serbia, whereas the witness said that they originated from Serbia and then fled back to Serbia once the campaign of arrests started.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I will also like to add that the prosecutor's office in Bijeljina, after a certain period of time, released all of them and they went back to Serbia. I think that we provided the MUP of Serbia with a list of individuals who had come from Serbia for whom we asked a ban on their entry to Republika Srpska. So after they had returned to Serbia, we provided them with the documents which ended in trials. One of them was Repic and he was sentenced to a prison term.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But that was in -- after the war, correct, in 1996?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't know when he was convicted, but I can categorically say that we provided the documents in 1992. Whether they processed Repic at a later stage by following him and applying all the regular police measures ending in a criminal report, but if you say that it was in 1996, then you must be right. All I know is that whatever documents we had available, we passed them on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have D1 -- 01581 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And before we look at the document in more details, I -- I just want to remind you that in your testimony - and that starts at 21499 - you describe the situation of the Muslim population in Janja and the measures that you took to protect them. And we do not need to repeat that. Just one question in this regard. The Muslims in Janja, they needed protection against Serb soldiers and the Serb formations that we just spoke about, correct, like Mauzer and Arkan's and those?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I know that upon Mr. Davidovic and I arrived in the area, our assessment was that the remaining Muslim population in Bijeljina deserved to be protected. We even offered an alternative. There was a man whom we helped to leave Janja. He was working in the police and we offered him to be a deputy chief of the police station in Janja because we set up a police station there. He refused that offer and instead asked us to help him cross over to Serbia and further on into Europe. Before we came, Arkan had been in Janja and I can say that with full responsibility and that he collected his dues - if I may put it that. There were constant attacks on civilian populations - and I mean Muslims or Bosniaks - who remained in Janja. In order to protect these residents, we set up a police station there and we provided command personnel and their permanent task was to provide protection of the property and the personal belongings and the lives of the citizens there. Now, as far as that period is concerned, I can say that we did it rather successfully. Now, whether any member of Mauzer's unit was in the area attempting to do something, I don't know. I told you about Arkan. I told you that I know that he had been there before our arrival and that he collected the valuables there, and after that we established regular authorities and restored law and order and provided the protection for the residents. Now, let me tell you something else. I do not hold Mr. Mauzer in high regard, but I'm unwilling to speak about something that I don't know about. If you put some specific questions about his activities, I will tell you what I know. Although I don't appreciate him too much, I would rather not talk about something relating to him that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And when we look here at that document, here it's a report you submitted to the Ministry of Interior on the 18th of July, 1992. And if we focus on the lower part, the lower part of the first page, you refer -- you refer here to areas where combat operations are not being conducted and the looting and war profiteering is taking place. I mean, you have already mentioned it here. That relates -- that's a pattern you saw in Brcko, Bijeljina, and Zvornik repeated; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know whether that was also repeated in other areas in the Republika Srpska, or rather, under control of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I know that we or I specifically in the latter part of August 1992, due to the worsened security situation and, so to speak, inappropriate vandalising of paramilitary formations, was supposed to establish a team and to go to Foca in order to re-install the legitimate authorities. I didn't go there for the reasons which are well-known, and I can tell you that if you wish me to do so --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's actually in your testimony. Therefore we do not need to go there. And other areas, you were not concerned, you never went or got information from the other areas under Serb control that this was a pattern, a general pattern?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it that way, that it was a pattern. But there were municipalities where security was compromised. As far as I can remember, there is mention of Bosanski Sabac, Foca, and when you interrupted me a minute ago this partly pertained to Lopare as well, where some of Manda's Chetniks were deployed. There was an instruction issued by the minister of the interior to set up a team that would intervene in all these "crisis" areas, where practically it was the paramilitaries who were governing the municipalities instead of legitimate organs. I was supposed to be the leader of one such team and I'm sorry that I didn't do that, although I could have risked my life, but I'm sorry that we did not restore law and order in the situations that it required.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, looking again at this document here, and in the English we would now need the second page while you have still the same page, you write here about -- that: "Despite the great efforts of members of the Security Service, the situation in Semberija at Majevica is being hampered by various political actions and trends, the effects of which are manifested through various attitudes towards the Service and the position of the Muslims, et cetera." The political trends and attitudes towards the service you have described in great detail in your testimony, and we leave that aside. The political action and trends and attitudes towards the position of the Muslims, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I'm going to make the following comment. Having read this last sentence, I'm not sure whether I would repeat it in the same way. But I think I put it correctly. The position of the Chetniks of Mirko Blagojevic who called upon the Muslims over the radio, asking them not to be afraid, et cetera, I can tell you that that was a counter-productive message because the very symbol of Chetniks, which was shown in every movie made after the Second World War, was a symbol of something dirty and something irregular. And this is what frightened the Muslims most, the people with long beards and cockades. And at that point in time, we assessed this to be counter-productive, because instead of stabilising their state of mind, they became more stressed and it worsened the situation on the ground. If I were to write this now, I don't know if I would have phrased it in the same ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You were aware that ethnic cleansing took place in April 1992 in Bijeljina, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I wasn't in the area. You have to know that I came to Bijeljina in early June of Bijeljina [as interpreted], and after that I was transferred to Brcko. I can confirm that the population did move out. There were even some murders. Later when we arrived in Bijeljina, Mr. Davidovic and I had established that there was some relocation of the populations, not to say that there was some ethnic cleansing but people were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your efforts to improve the security of the Muslims in Janja so that they would not have to leave, that was taken against you; right? You were blamed of protecting the Muslims and arresting Serbs. Is that not what happened and how it developed in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the reference? Who accused Mr. Andan and what is the source of this assertion?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is what Mr. Andan can actually tell us himself, and you know full well -- we all have read it in the testimony how he was removed. It's throughout the testimony, but I have asked Mr. Andan and there is no reference at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer your question in specific terms. Nobody from the then-government of Bijeljina municipality had anything against the way I operated. We had problems, the most serious problems, with Mauzer, Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer. We had problems with some Serbs because we wanted to abide by law to the letter. When we protected the Muslims of Bijeljina - and I reiterate that nobody from the government ever came and told us not to do that, instead there were people who lauded this method - but people started talking that Davidovic and Andan came to provide protection for the Muslims and they were arresting Serbs for stealing some small items. That was, if I may call it, a sort of propaganda war, especially against Mr. Savic [as interpreted], and it was being waged by Mr. Mauzer because the two had some unsettled problems dating from before the war. The problems started when Mr. Mauzer came from Belgrade and when I started doing my job - I don't want to repeat this - but I can say that this propaganda was being pursued by Mauzer against us and the groups who disagreed with the way things were done in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in line 25, it was not recorded that -- in his last answer as well it was not recorded what Mr. Andan said that, "We had problems with Serb criminals," not "Serbs."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People with the propensity to crime and criminal records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just also be reminded by my colleague here that in line 6 there is "Mr. Savic." It should be "Mr. Davidovic." It was definitely said in English, but the -- maybe it's a translation error.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the conflict was with Mr. Davidovic and Mauzer and not Savic with Mauzer basically so --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Especially -- especially this conflict involved Mr. Davidovic due to some earlier disagreements and unsettled accounts between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Andan, after you and Mr. Davidovic were removed from Bijeljina, the assaults against the non-Serbs, the murders and the looting, started up again. You're aware of this; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get the reference as to how Davidovic was removed and how Mr. Andan was removed? Davidovic ended his career and left his own republic --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we stop -- that is something that we can leave to the cross-examination [sic]. I'm not going to ask this because it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably Mr. Karadzic was challenging your statement that Davidovic was removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but he can take it up --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But he can call it up. I call it that. I put it to the witness that Mr. Davidovic and he were removed, and that is actually what the witness described in great detail in his testimony. That's why I used this term and the witness can answer the question. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please answer the question, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The then-federal secretary General Gracan issued an order and Mico Davidovic was transferred to Serbia due to the problems that he had with a Chetnik Vojvoda in Montenegro, the so-called Ceko. Together with his unit he was first transferred to Belgrade and then he was sent down there. And now if you want me to repeat, as far as I am concerned I --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the question was whether it was a removal or transfer, whether the assaults against non-Serbs, the murder, and the looting started up again. You were aware of this? This was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the interpretation was wrong. I'm sure you're not talking about the attacks against Serbs but against Bosniaks. What I received in the interpretation was "attacks against Serbs." I don't think that that's what you asked me. I have to say that at the beginning of September I was removed from the MUP because of the alleged taking of poker machines for private purposes. In my previous testimony I clarified that, so I don't want to repeat what happened. I joined the military and I went to Han Pijesak. I can't say whether the campaign of persecution of Bosniaks or Muslims continued in that area. I left very soon thereafter. Some people didn't even want me to stay in Bijeljina for any time, and I repeat that there was some people prone to crime, including Mr. Mauzer, who were at the forefront of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have evidence before this court - and I refer here to P5483 - that a huge number of Muslims were expelled from Bijeljina in August 1994 by the Serb authorities. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you tell me what period are you referring to? What part of August? Was it in the first half or the second half?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually continuing throughout August and also in September 1994. So it's a rather extensive campaign and, as we have seen in documents and heard also from Witness Davidovic, people were taken away -- taken forcibly from their houses and stripped of their belongings. They even had to pay large sum of money for transport. Are you aware of any such kind of things happening in 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Again, in the interpretation I heard the year 1994. I suppose that you're asking me about 1992. In the interpretation I heard the year 1994, but I don't think that that's what you meant. Was that a good interpretation, 1994, is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I was asking you about 1994. I'm aware that you were not there anymore, but it was widely known. So that's why I'm asking you. You either know or don't.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, I don't know. During that period, I didn't even pass through Bijeljina for certain reasons. One of them was the reason of principle. If Davidovic said that, he lived there, he had a house there, so you should have clarified that with him. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, do you know a certain Vojkan Djurkovic? Did you come across him in Bijeljina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Vojkan is not Djokovic but Djurkovic, if that's the person you have in mind. Mr. Davidovic and I came across him in 1992 in Brcko. He -- or rather, I was the first one who saw him there. Let's leave Mr. Davidovic aside. I arrived in Brcko to help the consolidation of the MUP or the public security station there. One day Mr. Djurkovic came to my office, Vojkan Djurkovic, and another person. I remember that he supported -- sported a moustache. He was a bit older. They introduced themselves as members of Arkan's unit. He, or rather, the two of them asked me to share with them the intelligence that I was privy to at the time. I don't know whether Mr. Vasiljevic was with me or not. I believe that he was. I told them that they didn't have any sort of legitimacy and that I sent my work reports to the Ministry of the Interior and that they did not have a legal basis to ask for any reports from me. That was when I met Mr. Djurkovic. I believe that I saw him once or perhaps two times when I was in Bijeljina, but those encounters were of no significance when it came to Mr. Djurkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware of criminal activities of Mr. Djurkovic, such as extorting money from people for transferring them elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I heard that indirectly. I heard that he was the number one man in Janja, that he forcibly took money and gold from Muslims. I personally didn't know about that. I didn't have first-hand knowledge. I could only hear about my friends or colleagues. I don't know when, but I suppose that it could have been in 1994, which is the year that you have -- kept mentioning. I can say that I did not have any first-hand knowledge about such activities of his. I did hear it from other people, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Andan, this morning you mentioned the -- how you got Mr. Vidovic released from Batkovic, and I was just wondering -- you said his name is not Anto but Avdo. Does that mean that he is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No. Actually, in the interpretation I heard the name Avdo and then I corrected that and I said that his name was Anto. I believe that even Mr. Karadzic intervened when he heard the name Avdo in the interpretation. It is not Avdo but Anto.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to confirm that. And Mr. Anto Davidovic -- Vidovic, he was not a criminal; right? And he was detained in Batkovic for the mere fact of being a non-Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No. He was a prominent athlete, a football player. His brother Zelimir Vidovic, who played for the Sarajevo football team, was even better known while Mr. Karadzic and I were in the club management. He is an older brother from Brcko. He remained living there, and when I asked certain people who were in Brcko at the time as to why he had been taken away from Brcko and put in the camp, they shrugged their shoulders and they said there was no reason. His wife was a Serb, but it seems that the only reason for that was the fact that he was a Croat. I don't even know who took him to Batkovic. He was a Croat and I invested a lot of effort, I used my personal connections, and I pleaded with the commander of the East Bosnia Corps for Vidovic to be released. He was released. I took him to Brcko and he found employment with the MUP of Brcko as an electrician. Now he lives in America. I found him employment in the MUP of Brcko. I told everybody that he was a good man, that he was good at what he did, and he stayed in Brcko until the end of the war as an employee of the Brcko MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We do not need to go into many details of Mr. Mauzer and the conflict that ensued. I just wanted to refer you to a document that is in front of this Trial Chamber and it's P2897. That is a report that you wrote in relation to an event on the 7th of July, 1992, at a celebration of St. John.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we briefly have that document, P2897, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2 you refer to Mauzer, Mauzer's forces, Serbian National Guard. And in the next paragraph you say: "Some people came to these areas. They were pro-Communist orientation ..." And then he says: "They are terrorising and mistreating the Serbian population on the territory of the Bijeljina municipality ... the police stop our warriors, they search them and confiscate worthless things and in this way abuse them." That is what was said by Mauzer, and Mauzer was actually an authority in Bijeljina; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, he was not a member of authorities there, but he was in charge of a very significant unit that was deployed there. Everything that you have just read out is correct. Some people came, allegedly they're communists, and that is reference to Mico Davidovic and myself. Let me repeat that they were not happy with the restoration of law and order, at least not fully. I'm sure that they swam best in that state of chaos and they could amass wealth. One night, an ambush was set up and in that ambush Mr. Davidovic and I were supposed to lose their [as interpreted] lives after we had visited Mr. Ilic in the command of the East Bosnia Corps. I'm sure that there are documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This Trial Chamber has seen such documents. And -- but Mr. Mauzer -- or rather, Mr. Savic, what his real name is, he was the head of the TO staff in Bijeljina, was he not? That's quite a high position.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I don't know, to be honest. I remember him as the commander of that unit of theirs. He was so dominant that he actually ruled all the segments of power and social life in Bijeljina. That's how I perceived his role. I don't want to speak ill of dead people, but let's say that his education was very modest, that he found himself in that place at that moment, and he wanted to cover all the bases. He wanted to be in charge of the complete situation there. That's the way I would put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we have evidence before this Trial Chamber - and that is the evidence of Mr. Davidovic, P2848 - that Mr. Savic and his men functioned as an escort to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik when they visited Bijeljina. Mr. Andan, were you aware of this? Was he escort?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: To be honest, I should be aware of the date. If that happened around the 17th or the 20th of August when I was removed from the position -- but I don't remember that it happened at that time. I really don't remember that during that period of time Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik arrived in Bijeljina, let alone who their escort was. I was in position up to the 17th of August and I have no reason not to tell you that I was aware of the situation if I had been.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We have also a document here in -- before this Trial Chamber, and that is P2855, in which Colonel Tolimir, then-Colonel Tolimir, in a report of the 28th of July, 1992, described the paramilitary formations as criminal elements doing all sorts of crimes. I do not want to go into all these details with you, but I want to quote one paragraph from this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 285 -- P02885 -- 2855, sorry, on the screen. And we need page 5 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S. And if we look at what is page 5 in both languages, and he goes into details about the Serbian -- yes, it's in the middle of the English and -- right in the middle and it is where you find Mauzer being mentioned in the B/C/S. Yeah, it's at the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it says here: "The Serbian National Guard in Bijeljina has formally joined the so-called Special Brigade. The Serbian National Guard was formed by the Bijeljina SDS, and the Presidency of the Bijeljina Municipality Assembly decided that this would be the army of Bijeljina which would defend Bijeljina should it be attacked, and appointed self-styled Major Ljubisa Savic ... Mauzer, as the commander." And then he writes - and that is in July 1992: "The greater part of the municipal authorities in Bijeljina still back the Guard." So Mauzer was not alone doing what he wanted. The greater part of the municipal authorities in Bijeljina still backed him; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: There is no doubt about the fact that he was very close to the authorities. We attended a meeting, Mr. Davidovic and I, and we informed about the situation in the Ministry of Defence. He came with two or three hand Motorolas. He contested our reports. I must confess the power structures did not support us, but they didn't even also provide comment about Mauzer's conduct at that moment. I believe that he should have been interrupted and that we should have been -- continued to go on informing the authorities about the situation. It is clear that he was close to the authorities, and about the first part, the SDS, I can't say anything about that. But I know from that meeting that he was close to the structures of power and that he behaved very badly towards Mr. Davidovic and myself when we came to inform the authorities about the situation in Bijeljina based on the information that we were privy to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have described your activity against the various paramilitary forces, and in particular the Yellow Wasps. And I'm just -- wanted to refer you to something that you said in your testimony, and that's at page 21868. You speak about that in relation to these Yellow Wasps, these persons, it went -- it was going round and round in circles. So you arrest them, they get released, they are expelled, and they come back, they are not prosecuted in Bosnia, or rather, Republika Srpska, they are not prosecuted in Serbia for a long, long time, and they roam around on both sides of the Drina River. Isn't that how it was for a long time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that was the situation and that situation prevailed for a long time. The people whom we expelled from Republika Srpska and handed over documents about them to the MUP of Serbia were banned from re-entering, but something else happened. They were intrigued by war and war developments and the loot that they were able to bring from the theatre of war. New such people appeared. We expelled one group, a ban was put on their re-entry, and then new people arrived which just picked up from where their predecessors left off. So, yes, things were going round and round in circles. And you're right when it comes to that. It was very difficult to control the situation. You complete one job, you process people, you transfer them across the Drina, you put a ban on their re-entry, but new people are recruited and appear. And that all lasted until the end of 1992. At least that's how I see that vicious circle of developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But that this vicious circle could develop, that's a matter of lack of political will to stop it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: You see, there is an expression for us police officers and those who speak our language will understand. I'm a policeman. My job is to catch the thief, to investigate the thief, and to hand him over to the court. And I believe that with that my part of the job is over. The moment when I hand them over to the prosecutor or to the court, my job is done. I'm not defending anybody; I'm here to tell the truth under oath. We learnt about war from books in peace time. What I learnt from books at the university was absolutely different from what I experienced in war time. We learned about the authorities that had -- have to be set up, about the police, about the military, but in our books there was no reference to any paramilitaries. When it comes to politics and political will, I know that the minister of the interior who was in office at the time and who was a political figure, we received very specific dispatches ordering us to investigate, to ban, and so on and so forth. It all depended on the chiefs of police in particular areas. They were in charge of implementing those dispatches and of their own willingness and initiative to prevent some things. I'm not talking about the government and the president because my minister was supposed to inform them about the situation. They were not supposed to receive information from elsewhere. And from my minister, who was also a political figure, we received dispatches with instructions, but then it all depended on the professionals on the ground, whether they would actually implement those dispatches, whether they would put words into action, whether they had the willingness and the initiative to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was my understanding - and we have heard that here in the courtroom and we have read it also in your transcript from the testimony - that you and Mr. Davidovic were such professionals who actually achieved results in very short time, but instead of letting you continue, you were stopped doing this, removed or taken elsewhere. Would you not think that's a lack of political will, to let the people continue who were doing a good job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Let me just provide a very short explanation. First of all, there were certain antagonisms within the top echelons of the Ministry of the Interior. I discharged duties as the chief of police in a municipality in Sarajevo, amongst other things, and that municipality was considered the most difficult from the security aspect, that was Stari Grad. At that time, Mr. Kovac was the deputy commander of the police station, and then I became the chief inspector at the republican MUP and he was still there. During the war something else happened. He was appointed first the chief of that police station and then the chief of administration, and I believe that in that situation he didn't like me. He was bothered by me being in that position. I was a professional and he didn't like that. So my removal or my departure from the ministry was the result of Mr. Kovac's personal attitude towards me. I had to be removed and replaced by one of his yes-men. The municipality of Bijeljina is on the border with Serbia. It's a transit municipality and gives a lot of room for a lot of things. And since I have to have -- I had -- didn't have blinkers, I wanted to do my job professionally, I bothered some people who were my superiors. That is the answer to your question. They made up some poker machines that I allegedly took and, luckily enough, I had ample documents to prove that the allegations were false. And this is all I can say about that. But to be honest, I have to tell you that I really regret that I didn't stay in the ministry as a professional. In 1993, or rather, in 1994, when Mr. Stanisic returned to the ministry, I was invited to set up a unit which would fight against crime. I'm sure that you're aware of that; you have documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, we actually have it also in the testimony. Let me speak with you about the Yellow Wasps in relation to one aspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I also can already see that I'm probably not able to -- I think I have used one and a half hours -- oh, I have one -- one hour left. That is sufficient, yes. Sorry. I just thought I had only half an hour left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.25. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, this morning you gave a few details on the transfer of Malko Koroman and why it was done and how it was done. I would like to ask you a few questions in this regard. In your previous testimony you mentioned that the Yellow Wasps received weapons from Malko Koroman at some point in time; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if I understand your evidence correctly, it was in relation to a deal for Golf cars that the Yellow Wasps had confiscated at one of their check-points; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was a service -- a favour for the fact that the Wasps returned these vehicles and in exchange for that favour he gave them some sort of weapons, Koroman did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these Golf cars, that was something, let's say, irregular. Transferring the Golf cars to Serbia, that's not proper, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I don't know details concerning this case. There were quite a few Golfs that were transferred from Vogosca, the TAS there, to Serbia irregularly. It was done by individuals or groups who stole the vehicles, had them transported to Serbia, and sold them there. As for this case involving Malko Koroman, I cannot state for a fact that these were stolen vehicles. At any rate, they chased the drivers away and took the vehicles for themselves. Malko Koroman came to see them, persuaded them into returning the vehicles, and in exchange for that he provided them with an amount of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Weapons, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on the occasion when the Yellow Wasps collected the weapons in Pale, they were received by Ms. Plavsic; correct? That's what you stated in your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: This was a misunderstanding. When we prosecuted the Yellow Wasps, or rather, we collected information that we forwarded to the prosecutor's office, after a period of time since they were released from detention and no proceedings had been initiated against them, they went to Pale and that was when Mrs. Plavsic received them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. You said that Koroman was not involved in anything criminal this morning, if I correct -- remember correctly, but Koroman was involved in this Golf car business and he provided weapons to Yellow Wasps at a time the authorities were aware of their criminal conduct. So there was a legitimate reason of the minister of interior to remove him; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I cannot claim this with any certainty either. I don't know who the vehicles belonged to. Perhaps it was on behalf of some of his friends or relatives that he interceded to have these vehicles returned. I can confirm, however, that once these vehicles were given back, these individuals went to Pale and were given a certain amount of weapons from Mr. Koroman. So I cannot claim that he was involved in any criminal activities surrounding these Golf cars because I don't know the background. I don't know who they belonged to. The fact of the matter remains that they received a certain amount of weapons from Mr. Koroman who had to take these weapons from the TO depot in order to be able to give them to him -- to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My question was actually whether -- if someone, leaving out the Golf cars, if someone provides weapons to a criminally active group, that's a legitimate reason to remove him from the police; right? It is not just a matter of not being effective; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Look, the fact that you have knowledge of this is the basis of the information we had. When he left the -- when I left the post in Bijeljina, it was up to Kovac to decide whether to file a criminal report and have Mr. Kovac prosecuted -- have Mr. Koroman prosecuted. So that question should have been put to Mr. Kovac. Because at any rate, we had to launch this initiative in the direction of Mr. Mico Stanisic. He could not have done it himself. He was at the top of the pyramid. It is up to these levels further down to launch this initiative up the chain since we weren't able to do it, but it was up to Mr. Kovac and Petko Budisa to launch this initiative to have him removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, to solve and calm down the situation in Pale at that point in time, it may be practical to remove him from the scene for a while, but to promote him and give him a position in the Ministry of Interior, that is not a proper way to deal with someone who has failed his job, his professionalism, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Look, after all this was not peacetime. There was a war. I heard somewhere of an English term for this. When you went to get rid of someone, when you want to kick him in the back and just to do it that way. I think this is how the situation unfolded with Mr. Koroman. The situation calmed down and there was no conflict between the two factions, one of which protected Mr. Koroman. And he was, conditionally speaking, given some sort of promotion by being sent to Pale. But the basic idea was that he should be removed from there. I think that was the objective and the whole purpose of his removal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you just said to be removed to Pale, that's probably a mistake, Bijeljina you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, he was at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: He was the commander at Pale and was removed and went to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he should be removed from Pale so that he may have no influence over the police station in Pale, and that bit about the influence over the police station in Pale was not reflected at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm, sir, having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said. Mr. Karadzic rightly intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25230 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that's again the transcript of the taped interview that you gave to the OTP in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to have e-court page 3 in English and we look at middle and below, and e-court page 4 in the B/C/S and we look at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I only address this very briefly for context. You refer here to the fact that you were removed from your position because somebody did not like you -- your work and you mention Ljubisa, Mauzer, as the primary person wanting this and you also mention Tomo Kovac. We do not need to address these two people because you have spoken about them in your testimony. You have spoken about them today. I only show it to you for context.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we move the -- we need to move in the English to page 4 and we -- the B/C/S is correct. We can stay with page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we look at the top part of the English and we look at the first half in the B/C/S. And here you say the following: "I also think that I stood in the way of a few politicians who also did not like such a situation. I think that this went all the way to the very top of the political leadership of Republika Srpska, to Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik ..." That is what you said in 2006. It was your belief then that it was also the Serbian -- Bosnian Serb leadership who wanted you to be removed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Another name is mentioned here, Ratko. I don't know who that would be. I can see Mr. Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik if I'm reading this correctly, the transcript in the first passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: "Mr. Radovan Karadzic, Ratko ... and Momcilo Krajisnik"; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Correct. I did say that but that was within a context, and if you want to you can review that transcript. I said that the leadership itself was not timely informed of certain things. So the impression gained was that the top leadership was not dealing with these problems adequately, including the problems that I was confronted with.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, can these two pages be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be -- these two pages will be added to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We come back to this point a little bit later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I see some difference between the B/C/S and English. In English at the end of -- after "Krajisnik," I read "that their duplicity."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's in the B/C/S before "Karadzic," because I'm not reading --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can explain this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since probably "Ratko" is missing, could we ask the witness to read out the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Duplicity is here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first passage, right, the first paragraph? "From the very top of Republika Srpska," is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "From the very top of Republika Srpska I think that it is to do primarily with the duplicity of Radovan Karadzic and Ratko ... and Momcilo Krajisnik." And that's what the document that I have reads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to explain something. What we have here and looking at here today are the two transcripts that were prepared, one in the English language and one in the B/C/S. There are sometimes slightly different wordings and that is how it was done at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. It's a transcription made on the audio recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25181 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is an article, or rather, an interview you gave entitled "Sting of the 'Yellow Wasps,'" and this interview was spoken about in your testimony in quite many details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that is at page 21796 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we do not need to go in many details. I just want to address two small aspects.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 2 in the English and we look at the right column, second paragraph. And page 2 in the B/C/S and we are looking in the B/C/S at the left column, second paragraph. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you are stated as saying that the direct cause for the operation in Zvornik was the fact that Velibor Ostojic had been stopped and humiliated. Mr. Andan, if I remember correctly, he was not only humiliated but his car was also taken from him, or is my memory failing me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: This was not the direct cause for the operation, what Mr. Ostojic experienced in Bijeljina at the time. We had been out in the field by then for some ten days gathering intelligence, perhaps even longer, about the whereabouts and activities of the members of the Yellow Wasps. This may have accelerated the whole process. Was his vehicle taken? Was it a Golf? I don't know. At any rate, he was humiliated at that check-point. I know that Rade Tanaskovic had a rifle, a pump shot-gun, I think, and he forced him to graze grass at that point. This was information we received from Velibor Ostojic and from Rade Tanaskovic's statement that we took later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The trigger or reason, whereas in line 11 it says "reason" or "cause." But what is the trigger or something that prompts something into action is not the same as the cause or the reason, which may be deeper. So it is true that this was not a reason but a trigger. This is what Mr. Andan said. As an illustration, the trigger for the breakout of World War I was the assassination on the archduke but that was not the reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What line are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 11 on page 75 [In English] "The direct cause of the operation" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original does not say "direct cause," it says what triggered or occasioned, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think his answer sufficiently tells itself. Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Andan, it is a fact that one or two days after this incident with Velibor Ostojic your operation against the Yellow Wasps was given the go-ahead, you could do it; right? There is a time context, is there not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: You must understand that every operative plan of the sort had to be approved by the MUP leadership. Perhaps it was the case that precisely in the days when Velibor Ostojic was being mistreated at the check-point, that we sent the plan operation for Bijeljina to Pale to receive approval for it. It is true that a day or two after the incident with Mr. Ostojic the operation was carried out in the manner already described and the individuals concerned were processed the way it was already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we move to page 3 in the English and we're looking at the left column and page 2 in the B/C/S stays and we are looking at the end of the paragraph that we just had before.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you refer here to the fact that you processed the case against the Yellow Wasps, but that no court verdict was known. And to say this in 2002. So again my question: There is -- there was no proper will to prosecute the Yellow Wasps of both sides of the Drina River at least for a long time; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I've already answered the question. I said that those of us from the ministry had done our part of the job. All the other measures and actions were in the hands of the prosecutor's office. It was up to them to act upon it. We were banned from interfering with other agencies' work and it was not our intention at the time or otherwise to interfere with the work of the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 25203 on the screen -- oh, Your Honour, I forgot. Can we have this article be admitted? It was addressed many times in various fractions in the previous testimony, but for some reason it was never tendered into evidence and I would like to do this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is being admitted, can the translation be revised, please? Secondly, the witness did not give his approval of what is stated in this interview. That's what he said. He didn't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a matter you may take up in your re-examination. We'll admit the -- this in its entirety, given that it is only seven pages. And then if there's a translation issue, there's a step you may take. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we assign the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6435, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 25203 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is the interview that Dusko Vukovic -- Vuckovic, aka Repic, gave on the 4th of August, 1992. It's taken by the military police, but I assume you are aware of this document, are you, Mr. Andan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Firstly, this isn't an interview, it's a statement. The interviews that we had would result in an official note, whereas this is an official statement that is noted down. This is the first time I'm seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this interview, or rather -- yeah, in this interview, in this official note of this interview, Dusko Vuckovic basically gives all the details of the crimes he committed in the Celopek camp. It's detailing the murders he committed and why he did it. You were not informed about this, this interview, and how he actually confessed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No. I'd be happy to receive this document. For my own sake, I'd like to have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's not possible for us to do. Okay. Then when you don't know it, I'm not tendering it, of course. I would like to move on to another topic that you basically addressed this morning, and that is the murder of Mr. Kulic in Bijeljina, and we also saw the information and the file that you prepared and the documents you prepared to investigate and prosecute this particular murder. And you also mentioned that the perpetrators were detained. But there were -- and you told us they were prosecuted only in 2006. I'm just wondering, who got them released and when? Why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I apologise, you said Kulic. Either interpretation was bad or at any rate it was Salko Kukic that this was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, I misspoke. I -- I mean this person, yes. The questions pertain to him.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I've already explained it. I said that we finished that part of the job, the police part of the job, very professionally. And I can tell you now, with the lapse of time, that I'm very proud of the job we did. We processed these individuals and handed them over to the prosecutor's office. They were taken into custody for 72 hours under the previously applicable Law on Criminal Procedure no longer valid. And the whole matter was handed over to the prosecutor's office. And this is where any further jurisdiction of a public security centre ceases. Why they weren't prosecuted, I don't know. I may have been mistaken about the year, but at any rate, I can tell you that based on that criminal report from 1992, these prisoners are today serving their sentence either in Bijeljina or in Banja Luka. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, what surprises me, most police officers - and we have a lot of them in our office - they care about the cases they investigate and they want to know what happens, what happens with their work. Are you saying you are not caring when you give it to the prosecutor's office, it's over for you, you don't bother anymore to inquire what happened with your file? Are you telling us that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, no. Of course I do care about having the individual in question prosecuted. There are records based on which one can check that indeed the prosecutor's office took into their jurisdiction the file and the individual, but since I left, I no longer had an opportunity to inquire and find out how far the case had gone. It would have been logical for me to do so had I continued working for the MUP in Bijeljina. In that case you could have rightly asked me, "Why didn't you send a single memo to them to inquire about the stages to which the case progressed?" But for the various reasons that I have already said - I will not repeat them - I no longer had the ability to inquire about these cases, just as I didn't have the opportunity to inquire about the case involving Yellow Wasps. Those who took up the position after I left had those case files on their desk and could have dealt with them, or rather, could have inquired about how far they progressed. Even in the communist regime we were banned from putting any pressure on the prosecutor. It was believed that once a case is put together and handed over to the prosecutor's office, the powers of the MUP cease. We could have answered questions that the prosecutor may have had of us and supplemented the case file if required to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever inquire informally with your former colleagues or in your position at the security administration in the VRS? I mean, there are ways. You didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: The very manner in which I left the MUP put an end to all my concerns and my interests. To put it simply, I just didn't want to inquire about any case that I dealt with previously. I didn't want to have any contact whatsoever with the MUP because I left the MUP feeling very irritated and that is when my interest stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's move on to Zvornik in relation to the planning of the operations against the Yellow Wasps, and I do not want to go into any details because you have given so many details in your testimony and there's no need for that and we also have your reports. I'm -- I only want to clarify one point. In your testimony at page 21473 you basically said that you planned and carried it out -- carried the operation out against the Yellow Wasps, and when you use the term "we," you sometimes use the term "we go" when you explained what was going on, and I think that -- is it correct that you mean Mr. Davidovic and you planned it and executed it with of course --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Correct. Mico Davidovic and I. And the forces with which he came to Bijeljina and the forces of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, that was a joint operation, a joint plan and implementation, and our assessment was that we needed the support of a special unit led by Mr. Milenko Karisik and we informed the Main Staff of the VRS who also provided some forces, but the latter forces did not take part in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I ask you this because Milenko Karisik, in his written evidence, at paragraph 31 of his statement under D3749, claims that he prepared the operation and he completed it successfully. What do you say? You smile, so what do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to use some abusive and foul words, but what he says is not correct. The whole operation was prepared by Mr. Mico Davidovic, Dragomir Andan and Goran Zugic who was the then-chief of national security in Zvornik. Due to the complexity of the situation, we invited a special unit led at the time by Milenko Karisik who did not take part in the operation, which I can confirm with full responsibility, and I would tell them the same thing to his face if we were -- if we were encountered.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I would now like you to see Exhibit P00036 on the screen. And it is your report dated 20 July 1993 in which you report on three paramilitary groups commanded by Zuco, Pivarski, and Niski. And you go into details of their strengths and the locations, the weaponry, and so on and so forth, but we do not need to go there because you have provided all this in your previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to go to page 5 in the English, second paragraph, and page 5 in the B/C/S, also second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you say here that: "Zuco carries out all his criminal acts in return for larger amounts of money exclusively with assistance of respective members of the Government of Serb Municipality Zvornik ..." To whom are you referring here? Who is in the boat with this Zuco?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: You have to make a correction. It's not the 20th of July, 1993. I think it should read 20th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I definitely meant to say "1992." I'm sorry when I said "1993." Of course 1992. But my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: We have established beyond doubt that Mr. Zuco had direct contacts with the chief of the legal administration department and that the two of them were involved in some [indiscernible] with driver's licences and licence plates for vehicles. Secondly, whether his name was Marko Pavlovic or is it his alias, I don't know. He was the commander of the TO staff at the time in Zvornik. Zuco had a close relationship with him. This is the two names that I remember at the moment who were members of the Zvornik authorities and Zuco was closely connected with them and involved in illegal transactions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just let me ask you, maybe I just forgot the name, but who is the chief of the legal administration department?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I can't remember, but to be honest, I must admit that I overstepped my authority to a certain extent during his arrest because I was very much affected in a bad way by seeing a policeman being involved in such transactions. So I must admit that I overstepped my authority by using physical force against him, but anyway I cannot remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Marko Pavlovic, you arrested him also, correct? "You" meaning you and Mr. Davidovic and the troops. You arrested him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: That is correct. We arrested him and we handed him over to the national security service and he was driven to Sokolac by car. When I made some further inquiries about him, I received information that he was sick, that he had epilepsy, and that he had a seizure during detention in Sokolac, as a result of which he was driven to Serbia and hospitalised somewhere. That's all I know. But it is true that we did arrest him because we established that he was directly linked with Zuco. And I also omitted to mention the chief of the police station, I think his first name was Marko, and he was another person who was closely connected to Zuco. Maybe he still is called Marko. He might still be alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know about the expulsion of the Muslims from Kozluk in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I personally have no information about that, but I believe that in preparation for these activities we heard some fragments of the story, but not the entire story, about the expulsion of Muslims from Kozluk. Therefore, I cannot give you a proper answer. I did hear some insinuations about that, but I have no specific information. It was in the month of June; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, no. At the time I was in Brcko and therefore I cannot give you a complete answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then I will not address this with you. In relation to Brcko, I wanted to ask you about a particular document, and let me just see --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is a document that's already before this Trial Chamber and it is P02889 and it is a report of Captain Cuturic from the Eastern Bosnian Corps command of the 29th of September, 1992. And as you co-operated to a certain extent with the Eastern Bosnia Corps and co-ordinated, did you meet Captain Cuturic? Would you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, this is the first that I hear of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We do not need to go into many details. He basically, in this document, shared the same views on certain paramilitary groups that you also had spoken about. I just want to refer you to -- one question. He refers to a Major Gavrilovic. Do you know this person, do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: There was a Gavrilovic, a commander of a Semberija Brigade, but I don't know his first name, whether it was Nedjo or not, I don't know. Anyway, I do know that there was a Gavrilovic, the commander of either the 1st or the 2nd Semberija Brigade. And if it is the one and the same person, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because here this captain refers to Mauzer and Major Gavrilovic with Arkan's men led by Peja came to Brcko at some point in time in May. You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I cannot speak about the month of May because I came to Brcko on the 12th of June or 15th of June. Anyway, the date can be checked in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the last paragraph on this page here, he refers to the testimony of an Orthodox priest, Slavko, who described how Muslims and Croatian people were taken out and killed in front of their houses. And I quote, he says: "Such liquidations were committed unprofessionally and publicly and were available to everyone." Did you hear about this massacre that he is referring here to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't. In one of my testimonies when I was asked about Jelesic, I said what I had learned about him. And during my stay there two or three days later, due to the measures that we undertaken, Jelesic fled to Bijeljina. Now, as for these public executions, this is the first time that I hear about it. My primary task was to consolidate the police station in Brcko and hopefully I managed to do that and other people can confirm the same, and I am glad that it happened that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And while you were in Brcko, did you ever investigate mass graves of Muslim victims being murdered or Croats being murdered? Was that not one of your tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: That would have been one of my tasks had I remained in Brcko, but we say you build a house starting from the foundation. So my first task was to set up the police station, to fill the vacancies, and to fill the gaps that were left by the departure of Croats and Muslims, and only after that could I proceed with this procedure. So two or three weeks while I was there wasn't at all enough for me to investigate murders, rapes, and other dishonourable acts that were committed during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, considering your written evidence and the reports and that we have heard also from other witnesses about the events in Brcko, Bijeljina, and Zvornik you were involved in, your activities and your achievements in such a short time, one could have expected that you be rewarded during the events and not dismissed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I explained this a while ago. I told you what the main reason was, and that was Mr. Kovac's antagonism which was publicly displayed towards me. I tried to distance myself from that because of the strategic position of Bijeljina and the greater possibilities offering opportunities to those people to trade in oil and other goods. So the reason was not my inefficiency, and the documents show that both Mr. Davidovic and I did a good job there and there was no other reason except for the one I already mentioned. They even used as an excuse this poker machine. But they were just looking for something that would give them an excuse to remove me from my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And instead of rewarding you, a criminal like Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, was rewarded by Mr. Karadzic. You're aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I refer here -- Your Honour, I refer here to P2856, a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: What kind of reward are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have a video-clip where he's basically praised for his conduct and his achievements. You are not aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, I'm not. Trust me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the criminal Arkan parades his unit before Mr. Karadzic in Bijeljina and he's also praised, and I refer here to P2858. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that. I read about it only after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Koroman was kept in the police, even promoted, while you were removed. Zuco and this Branko Pavlovic were received by Ms. Plavsic. Would you agree that your establishment of law and order that allowed the Muslims to stay safely in Bijeljina and elsewhere and to arrest and remove the criminals, that was not appreciated by the Bosnian Serb leadership, and that's not just Mr. Kovac, it's the Bosnian Serb leadership. Isn't that the reality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Look, first of all, I don't know why several dismissals of ministers of the interior took place at all. It's not up to me to say why. I knew Mr. Stanisic even before the war. I had him in high regard as a professional, but he was succeeded by some people who never in their life were even near a police station. So one has to take all these circumstances into account. People who are leading an organisation need to know at least basic things about the Ministry of the Interior, and the policy-makers in the ministry are the most responsible for all the implementation of all measures on the ground. And that is what I see as a problem because all of a sudden an XY person comes, he had had no connection with the ministry before that, and he is now expected to create the policy of the ministry. I believe that had we had more professionals leading the ministry, the things in the -- on the ground would have been different. The policy-maker in the ministry is the minister, and he decides in which direction the ministry would go. Mico Stanisic - and I have no reason to defend him - during the most difficult period of lawlessness managed to establish certain structures of authority and managed to put out the worst fires in that period. I suppose that he would testify here and I suppose that you're going to ask him why he was dismissed. I don't know that, but in my view, some people who came after him, such as Ratko Adzic or this Rakic person, were persons who did not have proper training or skill and had no concept of what the MUP was and that's why we had problems on the ground. I cannot deal with the situation if I don't have any support from the leadership. During my tenure, I enjoyed the support of Mr. Stanisic, and not only I, everybody else. Just take a look at the dispatches sent by Mr. Stanisic during his term of office concerning the screening of criminals and other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Excellency. If I receive short answers, I hope we'll be able to end before the end of the session; if not, then we'll have to ask Mr. Andan to stay here over the weekend and come back next week. I would very much like you to ask him that, whether he would be bothered if he were asked to stay over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I arrived here to testify. I'm at your disposal, and you finish whenever you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that we started a bit -- ten minutes later, could we go on until 3.00 if possible?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, I'll start with last things first, those things which are freshest in your memory. Could you please tell us, when it comes to Mauzer, after the war was he certified by the international police? Did he have a position and what kind of position did he have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Not only Mr. Mauzer. All of us active members of the Ministry of the Interior were vetted by international organisations and we were certified by them. Mr. Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, were also under the certification process and he was the assistant minister for the policing matters after the war. I believe that it was in 1998 but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could he become that, if we leave aside his character and nature, if he had been a proven criminal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, without a conviction, he could not have not been certified. He should have been sentenced first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you say that Mauzer and his fighters were absolutely equal to Arkan and his fighters? Were the units the same as their commanders or perhaps you can tell us something different about those units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that the two were completely equal. I can't say that Mr. Mauzer equalled his unit. As far as I know, his unit was most active when Mauzer was not there, when his deputy was in charge. What I know about his unit is that his unit was successful in war time, on missions, but when his deputy was in charge they were even more successful than when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 87 it says that you were supposed to be rewarded rather than dismissed. That's how the question was worded by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. From the first report that you sent to the liquidation of those situations in Brcko, Bijeljina, and Zvornik, were you demoted or promoted in service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: In objective terms, I would say that when I arrived in Semberija and Majevica it was as a senior inspector. My activities, particularly those activities that I carried out together with Mr. Davidovic, prompted the under-secretary Mr. Cedo Kljajic to promote me into the acting chief of the public security centre in Bijeljina. I perceive that as promotion because it was based on selfless and honest work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the planning of operations, you said that you planned these operations together. Would the commander of a unit have to plan that part of the operation that pertains to his unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
