utterances.text: Yes, one part of the operation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown an interview and you said that you didn't authenticate it. Would you repeat such an interview under oath?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I have to provide several explanations before I officially answer your question. In Sokolac, the chief of security centre Zeljko Markovic was killed. On behalf of the ministry, I went to Pale to -- where -- or rather, I was supposed to go to Pale to be in charge of the complete investigation. 100 kilometres away from Banja Luka my superior told me to go back because I was told that they couldn't guarantee my safety in Sokolac if I arrived there and if I were put in charge of the investigation. I entered a verbal conflict with the minister of the interior, Mr. Dragomir Jovicic, and I asked from him to tell me why I had been returned. How could somebody call the minister of the interior and tell him that they did not guarantee safety for an official arriving in Sokolac. I was irritated by the minister's answer, which was very brief. I went to report it and I gave an interview of my own will, mind you. I said in my previous evidence that nobody had ever asked me to authenticate the interview. You can check that. This is correct. If I were to give the same interview today, I would authenticate half of it and I wouldn't authenticate the other half perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it was said that you were supposed to be rewarded, do you remember whether we tried to talk to the minister of defence and the minister of the interior and to all the civilian ministers and that we failed with the ministry, and were you invited to come back to the MUP together with Minister Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I just tried to explain that a little while ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you further continue. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think that is a very leading question to say: Do you remember whether ... and so on and so forth. That's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, you mentioned that Adzic and Rakic were not successful as ministers. Were they civilians or were they appointed as ministers by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I said before the Trial Chamber that that was my personal opinion. They were civilians. As a professional I would like to share my opinion with you. I don't think that they were successful ministers, although they joined the ministry as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you and Minister Stanisic receive invitations to return to the MUP? Did you return after those two civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: In 1994, Mr. Stanisic was reinstated. He took over the Ministry of the Interior again. I don't know during what part of her mandate that happened, whether in the first half or the second half. I was invited in the Kikinda villa or Kikinda hotel at Pale. Mr. Stanisic invited me there and the chief of national security, Mr. Dragan Kijac was present during that conversation. I was offered an opportunity to re-join the Ministry of the Interior and Mr. Stanisic told me that he wanted me to set up a unit which would comprise about 120 men, that I should be in charge of that unit, and that I should set up an operations department and an analytical department which would counter all forms of crime and war crime, and he had in mind the crimes that were committed between 1992 and 1994, and that there is money for that unit and for all the equipment. I was supposed to select men. I was supposed to select the facility that we would occupy and that we would -- under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior and the chief of national security. I was taken by surprise. That was my prime feeling. But I was also very glad. At first I even -- I agreed. I believe that that was during the second half of Stanisic's mandate. I agreed. I consented to that proposal on a condition that I was allowed to choose my personnel, that nobody could impose people on me, that the national security vetted every person that was supposed to be a unit member, that they made sure that they didn't have a criminal record, and after that I was supposed -- I would have been ready to launch that unit's activities. Unfortunately, very soon after that Mr. Stanisic was removed. He returned to Belgrade and that unit never took off the ground. It was never even established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about that proposal for setting up such a unit, did it have anything to do with your mission in Brcko, Bijeljina, and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I suppose that that was indeed the case because Mr. Stanisic knew very well how we behaved and what we did in those three municipalities. Obviously being aware of all that, he invited me and he offered me the role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, we heard in this courtroom that Minister Ostojic was ill-treated. We heard evidence that the civilian authorities in Zvornik were also abused. What was your conclusion? Why did -- the Yellow Wasps and militaries were so adamantly against the civilian authorities? It has been suggested here that they were arrested because they were against the legitimate authorities. Do you have your professional opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No, no, they were not arrested only because of that. I told you that some of the authorities were directly connected to Zuco and I've even given you their names. But the main objective of ours was to neutralise the paramilitary unit which was involved in plunder, rapes, murders, and the expulsion of Muslims, and that was all proven by investigations. When Muslim houses could no longer be plundered because there were none to be plundered, they started robbing Serbian houses. They were not there in order to help Serbian fighters on the front lines. They were there to get rich. They destroyed the few factories that still worked and existed, and they created a situation of hopelessness in Zvornik so that both Serbs and Muslims were afraid to walk through the town at day and at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So who was the first to turn against whom? Was it them that turned against the authorities or was it the authorities that turned against them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: They opposed the legitimate authorities. According to some information, they wanted to replace the legitimate president of the municipality by somebody loyal to them. They also wanted to remove the president of the Executive Board. They even entered the structure of the police structures in Zvornik. The commander reported to Zuco more than he did to us, although he was supposed to be accountable to us and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When operative plans are drafted and when an operation is prepared, how long did that last? It was an operation after all, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Under normal war-time conditions -- rather, peace-time conditions, we were supposed to open a file. We were supposed to do all the checks for all the persons. We were supposed to gather evidence in respect of those persons. Due to war-time situation, we couldn't do that. We did a shortened procedure as it were. We met with the chief of national security, Mr. Davidovic, and I met with the late Goran Zugic who was already in Zvornik and he already had a lot of information, intelligence, and then we agreed. And that was perhaps 10 or 12 days before the operation started. Then we agreed that I personally with three operatives would change into civilian clothes, that we would enter Zvornik, and that we would take stock of all the facilities where those paramilitaries were billeted. We even crossed over the river Drina because they had certain houses and facilities where they stayed in the territory of Mali Zvornik. When we gathered all the intelligence that we needed, we embarked on the drafting of the operation plan, and it had to be comprehensive. It didn't have to include only the forces and equipment that we had at our disposal, but rather all of the other relevant information that was necessary in order to neutralise them without any major consequences. Fortunately enough, there were no consequences and those people were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it took some time; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the light of those circumstances, how do you see the humiliation of Minister Ostojic? Because it was suggested that that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: I said, when the Prosecutor asked me that, that that was not the key reason. Mr. Ostojic was at the check-point perhaps two or three days before we started the operation. I think that that may have sped things along. Maybe we should have spent some more time on planning, but we started implementation much sooner. But that was not the main reason, the ill-treatment and humiliation of the minister at the check-point was not the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it comes to providing security, did you know my security detail? Do you know who my security detail members were and whether they were MUP employees?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: When it comes to that matrix, if I can call it that, we adopted that matrix from the republican MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Obviously your security detail had to be operative, i.e., you had a team who collected intelligence about risks threatening your person. There was also the so-called physical security and those were your body-guards. Those lads that I knew were policemen even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: When a president was attending a meeting of sorts and he had his security along, who would be securing the event itself. Would that be the host of the event or would the president have his security do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, in addition to your close protection, your personal detail, there were those who had to secure the route. This was done by the relevant municipal MUP. Now, as for the venue where the president and his associates would be, the chief of security centre would be the one in charge of making sure that security's provided for that venue and its immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 50 it was suggested to you that the Muslims needed protection from Serbian soldiers and formations. Let me ask you this: These Serb "soldiers" and these Serb formations, did they have legality and legitimacy, as it were? Were the authorities firmly behind them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, firstly, the Muslims were unable to seek protection from the army. That part of the job fell upon the Ministry of the Interior. The army was at the front line and the police was in the town. I don't know which formations you had in mind specifically. If you meant paramilitary formations, they had no legitimacy whatsoever nor were they able to provide protection to the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I may have been unclear. The idea was that they needed someone to protect them from the Serb formations and soldiers. So this is my question: These people who endangered the Muslims, did they have the legality and the legitimacy that goes along with the Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you the Serb forces and those who co-operated with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Well, figuratively speaking I represent the state. The state has delegated me to carry out law enforcement jobs out in the field and I was doing that and members of the Ministry of the Interior were doing precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At page 36, at the start of cross-examination, it was suggested that agreements were reached between the various parties for appointments and positions. Can you tell us, did I interfere with the staffing policy or was it simply that I would receive information and it would be the Serb collegium that would propose candidates for these posts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN
utterances.text: Had that been the case you would have needed six more lives to allow you to solve all these problems. I know that you with Mr. Izetbegovic and, who was it, was it Kljujic, you of course arranged only for what was to be the Serb personnel and now it was the personnel services further down the line, your line, that would be dealing with these issues specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan. Apparently I don't have any more questions for you, as these are not pertinent. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, Mr. Andan, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will have to seize this opportunity to ask once more that measures be taken with regard to Milan Lukic, your detainee, from whom I keep receiving threats, myself and my family. Yesterday when I visited Mr. Karadzic, I was again threatened by Mr. Lukic, that he would liquidate myself and my family, and I'm appealing once more to you that measures be taken that Milan Lukic be prevented from telephoning my family in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a look into that with very much concern. We'll continue on Monday morning at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of July, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.48 p.m.,
